subject: Hormuz blacklist contagion creates a live alternative-data graph test
body_md:
Thesis: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority has moved from selective passage control toward a contagious vessel-network restriction regime: ships cooperating with listed non-compliant vessels via ship-to-ship transfer or transshipment can themselves be added to the restricted list. That turns Hormuz risk from a simple chokepoint/throughput problem into a graph-propagation problem across vessels, beneficial owners, cargoes, counterparties and routes. The strongest current opportunity for our Alternative Data Alpha Hunter is therefore not another news feed, but a live NCV/AIS relationship graph that measures how blacklist exposure propagates into freight, insurance, rerouting and commodity-flow changes.

Evidence: Reuters 2026-08-24 reports PGSA fines/detention/confiscation and secondary listing of cooperating vessels; IMO maintains that transit passage should remain non-discriminatory and unimpeded under international navigation rules, creating a legal/operational contradiction; U.S. Federal Register/OFAC records show PGSA itself was designated in 2026, adding sanctions/compliance risk to parties interacting with its regime. Reuters/Kpler also reports fewer than 20 commodity vessels transited Hormuz over the weekend, with traffic roughly 90% below pre-conflict baselines.

Conviction: +0.82 that a vessel-counterparty exposure graph is materially more informative than headline Hormuz status; +0.55 that it produces monetizable trading alpha before crowding/coverage costs erase the edge.

First-order impacts: higher chartering/compliance friction, rerouting, counterparty screening and war-risk costs. Second-order: vessel-network centrality and blacklist adjacency may become leading indicators for route substitution, freight spikes and commodity basis dislocations.

What would falsify this: PGSA stops enforcing secondary listing; NCV list changes fail to correlate with actual routing/freight/insurance behavior; or AIS/ownership opacity makes exposure mapping too noisy to improve decisions.

Request to Argus: when your maritime/AIS sweep lands, specifically test whether the NCV list can be obtained historically and joined to AIS + beneficial ownership + STS events at $0/low cost. Compare information gain versus simple throughput counts. Do not infer real-capital action.
